content.prompt: Which statement best describes cyber security?

options.label: Protecting information systems, networks and data from unauthorised access, damage or disruption
Only installing antivirus software on personal devices
Making websites load as quickly as possible
Printing paper backups of every email

feedback.correct: Cyber security is about protecting systems, networks and data — not speed or printing alone.
feedback.incorrect: Cyber security is about protecting systems, networks and data — not speed or printing alone.

content.prompt: Which CIA aim is mainly about preventing unauthorised viewing of patient records?

feedback.correct: Confidentiality protects information from unauthorised access or disclosure.
feedback.incorrect: Confidentiality protects information from unauthorised access or disclosure.

content.prompt: Which CIA aim is mainly about keeping clinic booking systems running when staff need them?

feedback.correct: Availability means authorised users can access systems and data when needed.
feedback.incorrect: Availability means authorised users can access systems and data when needed.

content.prompt: Changing appointment notes without permission mainly threatens which CIA aim?

feedback.correct: Integrity is about accuracy and trustworthiness of data — unauthorised changes damage it.
feedback.incorrect: Integrity is about accuracy and trustworthiness of data — unauthorised changes damage it.

feedback.correct: Phishing uses deception to manipulate people — a common social-engineering method.

metadata.title: What cyber security means

content.text: What cyber security means
Cyber security aims to protect information. Pick the statement that uses that idea accurately.

content.prompt: Which statement best defines cyber security for this unit?

options.label: Protecting information systems, networks and data from unauthorised access, damage or disruption
Printing every patient letter so nothing is stored digitally
Only blocking social media on staff phones

feedback.incorrect: The unit definition is about protecting systems, networks and data — not appearance, paper-only working or one control.

content.prompt: What is the purpose of cyber security aims such as confidentiality?

options.label: To protect information so the right people can use it safely and it stays trustworthy
To make every system slower so attackers lose interest
To guarantee that no incident can ever happen

feedback.correct: CIA aims describe how information should be protected. They do not promise that incidents are impossible.
feedback.incorrect: CIA aims describe how information should be protected. They do not promise that incidents are impossible.

metadata.title: CIA Triad Learning
metadata.summary: Learn and check the Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability triad.

content.text: CIA Triad Learning
The CIA triad — Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability — is a core way to talk about what cyber security protects. Match each check question to the aim it describes.

content.prompt: Confidentiality mainly means…

options.label: Only authorised people can access information
Data is never stored on any computer

feedback.correct: Confidentiality limits access to authorised users.
feedback.incorrect: Confidentiality limits access to authorised users.

content.prompt: Integrity mainly means…

options.label: Information stays accurate and has not been improperly changed
Passwords are written on sticky notes

feedback.correct: Integrity protects accuracy and trustworthiness of data.
feedback.incorrect: Integrity protects accuracy and trustworthiness of data.

content.prompt: Availability mainly means…

feedback.incorrect: Encryption is a common control supporting confidentiality.

metadata.title: Confidentiality in practice
metadata.summary: Recognise confidentiality: information is viewed only by those authorised to see it.

content.text: Confidentiality in practice
Confidentiality means information is not disclosed to anyone who is not authorised to see it. Patient records at Northbank are a typical example.

content.prompt: Which situation is mainly a confidentiality problem?

options.label: A receptionist reads a patient record with no clinical need
The booking website is offline so appointments cannot be made
A clinic letter is saved with the wrong clinic date
A printer runs out of paper in reception

feedback.correct: Unauthorised viewing of a patient record is confidentiality. Downtime is availability; a wrong date is integrity.
feedback.incorrect: Unauthorised viewing of a patient record is confidentiality. Downtime is availability; a wrong date is integrity.

content.prompt: Which wording best describes confidentiality?

options.label: Only authorised people can view the information
The information can be used whenever staff need it
The information has not been changed in an unauthorised way
The information is stored on paper

feedback.correct: Confidentiality is about authorised viewing. Availability is about being able to use the information; integrity is about it remaining accurate and unaltered without authorisation.
feedback.incorrect: Confidentiality is about authorised viewing. Availability is about being able to use the information; integrity is about it remaining accurate and unaltered without authorisation.

metadata.title: Integrity in practice
metadata.summary: Recognise integrity: information remains accurate and is not changed without authorisation.

content.text: Integrity in practice
Integrity means information is complete, accurate and has not been altered without authorisation.

content.prompt: Which situation is mainly an integrity problem?

options.label: Someone changes a clinic appointment time without permission
Staff cannot open the booking system at 9am
A visitor photographs a patient list on a screen
The clinic Wi-Fi password is written on a poster

feedback.correct: Unauthorised change to an appointment record is integrity. Being unable to open the system is availability; photographing a list is confidentiality.
feedback.incorrect: Unauthorised change to an appointment record is integrity. Being unable to open the system is availability; photographing a list is confidentiality.

content.prompt: Which wording best describes integrity?

options.label: Information remains accurate and is not altered without authorisation
Information is hidden from every member of staff
Systems are always faster than paper
Backups are stored in another country

feedback.correct: Integrity is about authorised, accurate information — not hiding data from all staff or where backups are stored.
feedback.incorrect: Integrity is about authorised, accurate information — not hiding data from all staff or where backups are stored.

metadata.title: Availability in practice
metadata.summary: Recognise availability: authorised people can use systems and data when they need them.

content.text: Availability in practice
Availability means authorised users can access systems and information when they need to. Northbank’s booking website is a typical example.

content.prompt: Which situation is mainly an availability problem?

options.label: Attackers flood the booking website so patients cannot book
A staff member emails a patient contact list to a personal account
A dosage field in a record is overwritten with the wrong number
A policy document uses everyday language instead of specification terms

feedback.correct: A flood that stops booking is availability (and matches denial of service). Sending a contact list is confidentiality; a wrong dosage is integrity.
feedback.incorrect: A flood that stops booking is availability (and matches denial of service). Sending a contact list is confidentiality; a wrong dosage is integrity.

content.prompt: Which wording best describes availability?

options.label: Authorised people can use the system or data when they need it
Nobody except the attacker can see the data
The data has been secretly changed
The organisation has printed a poster about passwords

feedback.correct: Availability is about authorised use at the time of need.
feedback.incorrect: Availability is about authorised use at the time of need.

metadata.title: Distinguishing CIA aims
metadata.summary: Sort short cases into confidentiality, integrity or availability.

content.text: Distinguishing CIA aims
Similar-looking problems can affect different CIA aims. Classify each case.

content.prompt: Which CIA aim is mainly affected?

items.label: A visitor reads patient names on an unlocked screen
An appointment note is changed to the wrong clinic
The booking website will not load for a morning
Staff copy a patient contact list without a work need
The booking service is flooded with fake requests

feedback.correct: Viewing or copying without authorisation is confidentiality. Unauthorised change is integrity. Not being able to use the service is availability.
feedback.incorrect: Viewing or copying without authorisation is confidentiality. Unauthorised change is integrity. Not being able to use the service is availability.

metadata.title: When more than one CIA aim is affected
metadata.summary: Spot when one incident can affect more than one CIA aim.

content.text: When more than one CIA aim is affected
One incident can threaten more than one aim. Name the aims that are clearly affected.

content.prompt: Ransomware encrypts clinic files so staff cannot open them, and a ransom note is left on screen. Which aims are clearly affected?

options.label: Integrity and availability of the files
Only the colour of the desktop wallpaper
Confidentiality of a public waiting-room poster

feedback.correct: Encrypting files changes them without authorisation (integrity) and stops staff using them (availability).
feedback.incorrect: Encrypting files changes them without authorisation (integrity) and stops staff using them (availability).

content.prompt: A stolen clinic laptop still contains a patient contact list. Which aim is the first concern?

options.label: Whether the clinic logo looks professional

feedback.correct: The contact list on a stolen device is a confidentiality concern. Other CIA aims may also be discussed later, but the list being readable by someone unauthorised is the first specification point.
feedback.incorrect: The contact list on a stolen device is a confidentiality concern. Other CIA aims may also be discussed later, but the list being readable by someone unauthorised is the first specification point.

metadata.title: Six incident types: definitions
metadata.summary: Match each of the six specification incident types to its meaning.

content.text: Six incident types: definitions

The specification names six incident types: hacking, virus, denial of service (DoS), phishing, identity theft, and data interception and theft. Use those names — do not substitute looser everyday labels.
Keyword bank: hacking · virus · denial of service (DoS) · phishing · identity theft · data interception and theft

content.prompt: Which incident type is unauthorised access to a system or account?

feedback.correct: Hacking is unauthorised access. DoS stops a service; a virus infects; phishing deceives a person.
feedback.incorrect: Hacking is unauthorised access. DoS stops a service; a virus infects; phishing deceives a person.

content.prompt: Which incident type uses a deceptive message to trick a person into giving information or access?

feedback.correct: Phishing is deception aimed at a person. A virus is malware; DoS floods a service; interception captures data in transit.
feedback.incorrect: Phishing is deception aimed at a person. A virus is malware; DoS floods a service; interception captures data in transit.

content.prompt: Which incident type captures or steals data as it is transmitted or stored?

feedback.correct: Data interception and theft is about capturing or stealing the data itself. Hacking is unauthorised access; DoS is disruption; a virus is malware.
feedback.incorrect: Data interception and theft is about capturing or stealing the data itself. Hacking is unauthorised access; DoS is disruption; a virus is malware.

metadata.title: Incident Classification
metadata.summary: Classify short Northbank scenarios into cyber security incident types.

content.text: Cyber Security Incident Types
Classify each short scenario as the most suitable incident type. Categories can overlap in real life — choose the best fit for formative practice.

content.prompt: Classify each incident scenario.

items.text: Staff open an email attachment that encrypts clinic files and demands payment.
items.explanation: Ransomware is malicious software — a malware incident.

items.text: A message claiming to be from IT asks reception to confirm their password on a fake login page.
items.explanation: Credential theft via a deceptive message is phishing / social engineering.

items.text: Attackers flood Northbank’s booking website so patients cannot book appointments.
items.explanation: Overwhelming a service so legitimate users cannot use it is denial of service.

items.text: A leaving member of staff copies patient contact lists they are not allowed to take.
items.explanation: Misuse by someone with insider access is unauthorised access / insider misuse.

items.text: A stolen clinic laptop is taken from an unlocked staff room overnight.
items.explanation: Theft of a device from premises is a physical security incident.

items.text: Someone pretends to be a delivery courier to walk into a restricted records area.
items.explanation: In-person deception to gain entry is social engineering (not malware).

feedback.correct: Those scenarios match the expected incident types.
feedback.incorrect: Check whether the main issue is malware, deception, service denial, insider misuse, or a physical event.

content.prompt: Explain one classification. Name the scenario, the type you chose, and one clue in the wording that led you there.

metadata.title: Recognise the incident from the scenario
metadata.summary: Name the specification incident type from a short scenario.

content.text: Recognise the incident from the scenario
Read the evidence in the scenario, then name the incident type. Do not invent extra facts.

content.prompt: Staff open an email attachment. Clinic files will not open and a payment demand appears. Which incident type is this?

feedback.correct: Malware that infects files is a virus incident. The payment demand describes ransomware behaviour, which is still malware/virus in this unit’s incident list — not phishing by itself.
feedback.incorrect: Malware that infects files is a virus incident. The payment demand describes ransomware behaviour, which is still malware/virus in this unit’s incident list — not phishing by itself.

content.prompt: A message claiming to be from IT asks reception to confirm a password on a fake login page. Which incident type is this?

feedback.correct: A deceptive message asking for a password is phishing. Hacking would be the unauthorised access that might follow if the password is used.
feedback.incorrect: A deceptive message asking for a password is phishing. Hacking would be the unauthorised access that might follow if the password is used.

content.prompt: Attackers flood Northbank’s booking website so patients cannot book. Which incident type is this?

feedback.correct: Flooding a service so legitimate users cannot use it is denial of service.
feedback.incorrect: Flooding a service so legitimate users cannot use it is denial of service.

metadata.title: Tell similar incidents apart
metadata.summary: Separate incident types that learners often mix up.

content.text: Tell similar incidents apart
Phishing is not the same as hacking. Identity theft is not the same as data interception. Choose the precise type.

content.prompt: Someone uses stolen credentials to open a staff mailbox. Which incident type is this mainly?

feedback.correct: Using stolen credentials to open a mailbox is unauthorised access — hacking. Phishing would be the deceptive message that obtained the credentials, if that was what the scenario described.
feedback.incorrect: Using stolen credentials to open a mailbox is unauthorised access — hacking. Phishing would be the deceptive message that obtained the credentials, if that was what the scenario described.

content.prompt: Criminals open a credit account using a patient’s name and date of birth copied from a list. Which incident type is this mainly?

feedback.correct: Misuse of identity details is identity theft. The copying of the list could also be data theft, but the question asks what happens when those details are used as someone else’s identity.
feedback.incorrect: Misuse of identity details is identity theft. The copying of the list could also be data theft, but the question asks what happens when those details are used as someone else’s identity.

metadata.title: Evidence for a classification
metadata.summary: Choose the evidence that justifies an incident classification.

content.text: Evidence for a classification
A classification is only as strong as the evidence in the scenario. Pick the phrase that actually justifies the type.

content.prompt: You classify a case as phishing. Which evidence best supports that?

options.label: The message pretends to be from IT and asks staff to enter a password on a fake page
The booking website is slow on Monday mornings
A laptop charger is missing from a drawer

feedback.correct: Phishing needs evidence of deception aimed at a person. Using email, or a slow website, is not enough.
feedback.incorrect: Phishing needs evidence of deception aimed at a person. Using email, or a slow website, is not enough.

content.prompt: You classify a case as denial of service. Which evidence best supports that?

options.label: Legitimate patients cannot use the booking site because it is flooded with fake requests
A staff member opened one attachment
A password was typed on a fake page
A contact list was emailed to a personal account

feedback.correct: DoS evidence is that the service cannot be used by legitimate users because of flood or disruption — not deception or data copying.
feedback.incorrect: DoS evidence is that the service cannot be used by legitimate users because of flood or disruption — not deception or data copying.

metadata.title: Incident type and CIA aim
metadata.summary: For each scenario, name the incident type and the CIA aim mainly compromised.

content.text: Incident type and CIA aim
Each question asks for a pair: incident type and CIA aim. Use specification names.

content.prompt: A fake payroll email harvests a reception password. Which pair is best?

feedback.correct: The deceptive email is phishing. The password, if used, exposes accounts and data — confidentiality.
feedback.incorrect: The deceptive email is phishing. The password, if used, exposes accounts and data — confidentiality.

content.prompt: The booking website is flooded and patients cannot book. Which pair is best?

feedback.correct: Flooding the service is DoS. Patients cannot use booking — availability.
feedback.incorrect: Flooding the service is DoS. Patients cannot use booking — availability.

content.prompt: Malware changes clinic files so they will not open. Which pair is best?

feedback.correct: Infecting and altering files is a virus incident. Files that will not open have lost integrity and availability.
feedback.incorrect: Infecting and altering files is a virus incident. Files that will not open have lost integrity and availability.

metadata.title: Justify a paired classification
metadata.summary: Write a short justification that names the incident type, CIA aim and evidence.

content.text: Justify a paired classification
Sentence starters: The incident type is… because… The CIA aim mainly affected is… because the evidence shows…
Scenario: A courier asks reception to ‘hold the door’ and then photographs a patient list on an unlocked screen in the staff room.

content.prompt: Which incident type best fits this evidence?

feedback.correct: Photographing the list is taking data. That is data theft. It is not a flood, malware or a deceptive email.
feedback.incorrect: Photographing the list is taking data. That is data theft. It is not a flood, malware or a deceptive email.

content.prompt: Justify your classification. Name the incident type, the CIA aim mainly compromised, and the evidence in the scenario. Do not add facts that are not there.
content.guidance: Name type, aim and evidence. Keep to the scenario.

content.prompt: Which statement best describes cyber security?

content.prompt: What does confidentiality mean in the CIA triad?

options.label: Information is available whenever authorised users need it

Information is never changed once it has been saved
Information is backed up to an off-site location

feedback.correct: Confidentiality means only authorised people can view or obtain the information.
feedback.incorrect: Confidentiality means only authorised people can view or obtain the information.

content.prompt: What does integrity mean in the CIA triad?

options.label: Information is accurate and has not been altered without authorisation

Information is shared only inside the organisation

feedback.correct: Integrity means information remains complete, accurate and trustworthy.
feedback.incorrect: Integrity means information remains complete, accurate and trustworthy.

content.prompt: What does availability mean in the CIA triad?

feedback.incorrect: Availability means authorised users can access systems and data when required.

feedback.incorrect: Personal data must be protected to reduce harm to individuals and to meet legal and ethical duties.

feedback.incorrect: Organisational data supports services and decision-making; compromise can halt operations and damage trust.

metadata.title: Impacts: loss, disruption and safety
metadata.summary: Learn loss, disruption and safety, then apply them to short cases.

content.text: Impacts: loss, disruption and safety

Loss means something of value is taken, damaged, corrupted, or no longer trusted. That includes confidentiality (the wrong people can see information), integrity (information is no longer accurate), availability (a system or record cannot be used), money, identity, reputation and confidence.
Disruption means a service people depend on stops, slows, or becomes unreliable. OCR examples include healthcare, transport, broadcasting, utilities, oil installations and traffic control.
Safety means people are placed at greater physical risk. A delayed clinical review or unsafe traffic signals can be a safety impact, not only a financial one.
One incident can create more than one of these. Name who is affected and use evidence from the scenario.

feedback.incorrect: Booking that cannot be used is disruption of a service people depend on. Overtime is financial loss. News coverage is reputational. Misused identity details are a loss for the individual.

feedback.incorrect: A delayed time-critical review increases physical risk for that patient. News coverage is reputational. The invoice is financial loss. An unopened drive is loss of availability and disruption.

metadata.summary: Classify impact statements as loss, disruption, safety, or more than one category.

content.text: Loss, Disruption and Safety Classification
Classify each statement as Loss, Disruption, Safety, or More than one category. Use More than one category when a justified combination fits.

content.prompt: Classify each impact statement.

items.text: Northbank pays emergency contractor fees to rebuild encrypted servers.
items.explanation: Direct extra spending is financial loss. It does not, by itself, describe a stopped service or physical risk.

items.text: Clinic booking services are unavailable for two working days, so reception cannot confirm visits.
items.explanation: This is clearly disruption of a depended-on service. Some learners may also argue loss of availability; if you chose more than one category, your reason should identify the service and who depended on it.

items.text: A patient’s urgent review is cancelled because Northbank cannot access records; the delay increases clinical risk for that patient.
items.explanation: Physical or clinical risk to the patient is a safety impact. It may also be disruption for the organisation. More than one category is defensible when both perspectives are explained.

items.text: Stolen patient identity details are later used to open fraudulent accounts.
items.explanation: Identity theft is a loss impact for the individual. Focus on what the person lost or had misused.

items.text: Local news coverage leaves patients unsure whether Northbank can be trusted with medical information for months afterwards.
items.explanation: This is reputational loss / loss of customer confidence. It may be hard to quantify but remains an important longer-term loss impact.

items.text: Interference with a traffic-control system causes unpredictable signal behaviour on major routes used by ambulances.
items.explanation: The service becomes unreliable (disruption) and people may be placed at physical risk (safety). More than one category is often the strongest justified choice.

items.text: Partner clinics pause referrals while they check whether shared patient records can still be trusted.
items.explanation: Paused referrals disrupt how the organisations work together. The reason is also a loss of trust in the records. Either emphasis can be justified, so more than one category fits.

items.text: An oil installation’s control systems are taken offline and normal operations stop.
items.explanation: Stopped operations are disruption. Safety may also be argued if the scenario evidence shows people placed at physical risk; do not invent hazards that are not stated.

feedback.correct: Those impact statements match the expected categories.
feedback.incorrect: Check whether each statement is mainly loss, disruption, safety, or more than one.

content.text: Spot the impact
A college's student records system is encrypted by ransomware on Monday morning. Staff cannot access timetables, attendance records or student contact details for two days.

content.prompt: Classify each statement.

items.text: Staff cannot open timetables or attendance records.
items.explanation: Staff cannot use a service they rely on. That is disruption.

items.text: Student contact details cannot be accessed for two days.
items.explanation: The contact details cannot be used when needed. That is loss of availability.

items.text: Students may miss classes because staff cannot contact them.
items.explanation: Students missing classes is disruption of their learning. The scenario does not describe physical harm, so this is not a safety impact.

items.text: A regulator has already fined the college.
items.explanation: The scenario does not say a fine has been issued. Do not add impacts that are not supported.

content.prompt: Identify two impacts of this incident. For each one, give one piece of evidence from the scenario.

The website is taken offline while the company investigates

metadata.title: Immediate and longer-term consequences
metadata.summary: Classify consequences by timescale and complete an impact chain.

content.text: Immediate and longer-term consequences
Some consequences happen at once. Others appear later. A consequence can reasonably fit both, depending on the scenario.

content.prompt: Classify each consequence.

items.text: The booking system cannot be opened on the morning of the attack.
items.explanation: The system is unavailable as the incident starts.

items.text: Staff cannot see that day's appointments.
items.explanation: The effect is on the clinic that day.

items.text: Investigation invoices arrive over the following months.
items.explanation: The cost continues after the first day.

items.text: Fewer patients book routine appointments six months later.
items.explanation: Lost confidence shows up after the systems are back.

items.text: Local news reports the outage the same day, and patients still mention it months later.
items.explanation: The report is immediate. The effect on confidence can continue. Either timescale can be justified if you say which part you mean.

items.text: The organisation later changes how backups are stored.
items.explanation: A change to process comes after the incident, not at the moment systems fail.

metadata.title: Improving insecure implementations
metadata.summary: Choose a secure alternative for each fictional Northbank snippet and explain one root-cause fix.

content.text: Improving insecure implementations

Each item shows a deliberately insecure training snippet, then asks you to choose a secure alternative. The goal is to fix the root cause (how data and access are handled), not to hide one example string. All data is fictional.
These snippets are incomplete on purpose. They only need to show that the weakness exists. Do not extend them into working attacks, and do not copy them into production systems.

content.prompt: Insecure training lookup: query = "SELECT * FROM training_patients WHERE surname = '" + typedSurname + "'". Which rewrite is the secure alternative?

options.label: Escape quote characters, then still join the surname into the query text
Use a parameterised query so the surname is bound as data, not mixed into the SQL text
Move the query into a longer function name
Show the finished query on the page so staff can read it

feedback.correct: Parameter binding (or an equivalent ORM API) keeps untrusted text out of the SQL structure. Filtering a few characters is brittle and is not the root-cause fix.
feedback.incorrect: Parameter binding (or an equivalent ORM API) keeps untrusted text out of the SQL structure. Filtering a few characters is brittle and is not the root-cause fix.

content.prompt: Insecure training page: comments.innerHTML = visitorMessage. Which rewrite is appropriate?

options.label: comments.textContent = visitorMessage (or another encoding-safe output method)
Encode the message, then still assign it with innerHTML
Save the message in localStorage and still assign innerHTML

feedback.correct: textContent (or auto-escaping templates) treats the message as text. Doubling innerHTML or relying on CSS does not fix unsafe HTML insertion.
feedback.incorrect: textContent (or auto-escaping templates) treats the message as text. Doubling innerHTML or relying on CSS does not fix unsafe HTML insertion.

content.prompt: Insecure training config: CLINIC_DEMO_TOKEN = "not-a-real-secret" committed next to the app. What should happen?

options.label: Keep it in the file because the name says demo
Remove it from the file, load secrets from a secret store or environment at run time, and rotate any value that was copied
Rename the variable and commit the same file
Copy the token into the project README

feedback.correct: Secrets must not travel with source copies. Rotate anything that was exposed, even in a demo, so the old value cannot be reused.
feedback.incorrect: Secrets must not travel with source copies. Rotate anything that was exposed, even in a demo, so the old value cannot be reused.

content.prompt: Insecure records route: return trainingRecord(idFromUrl) with no further check. What is the secure alternative?

options.label: Load the record only if the signed-in clinician is authorised for that patient or role
Use a longer identifier and still return any matching record
Log the access, then still return any matching record
Cache every training record in the browser for speed

feedback.correct: Object-level authorisation is the root-cause fix. Longer IDs (obscurity) do not replace an access check.
feedback.incorrect: Object-level authorisation is the root-cause fix. Longer IDs (obscurity) do not replace an access check.

content.prompt: Insecure kiosk setup: a shared admin / admin login on the training terminal. What is the secure alternative?

options.label: Unique accounts, no default passwords, and MFA where the platform supports it
Change the shared password and give it to every member of staff
Keep one shared login but change the username
Leave the shared login and turn off the screen lock

feedback.correct: Shared defaults are the weakness. Unique credentials and extra factors reduce the chance that one leaked password opens the kiosk.
feedback.incorrect: Shared defaults are the weakness. Unique credentials and extra factors reduce the chance that one leaked password opens the kiosk.

content.prompt: Insecure share: Everyone (clinic Wi-Fi) = Read on the draft-letters folder. What is the secure alternative?

options.label: Restrict the share to the staff group that needs those files; keep guests off that folder
Add more files to the same open share
Rename the folder and leave the same read permission
Move the letters to a second folder with the same open permission

feedback.correct: Least privilege on the share is the configuration fix. Renaming or hiding files does not change who can open them.
feedback.incorrect: Least privilege on the share is the configuration fix. Renaming or hiding files does not change who can open them.

content.prompt: Choose one insecure snippet. Explain the weakness, the possible impact for Northbank, the secure alternative you chose, and one way a reviewer could detect a regression. Do not include attack steps against a real system.
content.guidance: Cover weakness, impact, fix, and detection. Fix the root cause, not one example string.

content.text: Choosing defensive controls

A control reduces risk by removing a weakness, limiting a threat, or reducing impact. Pick the control that best fits each fictional Northbank situation. Prefer the control that treats the root cause, not a single symptom.

content.prompt: Match each situation to the most appropriate defensive control.

items.text: The kiosk still runs last year’s booking component after the vendor issued a fix.
items.explanation: Apply the vendor fix and keep a version inventory. Patching treats the unpatched-software vulnerability.

items.explanation: Check that the signed-in user is allowed to see that record (object-level authorisation).

content.text: Vulnerability, threat and risk
Classify each statement as a vulnerability, a threat, or a risk. Then write one Northbank chain that uses all three terms.

content.prompt: Classify each statement as a vulnerability, a threat, or a risk.

items.text: The training booking app concatenates surnames into a SQL string.
items.explanation: This is a weakness in how the app is written.

items.text: A criminal group that tries to steal clinic appointment data for fraud.
items.explanation: This names who might cause harm, not the weakness itself.

items.text: If the unpatched kiosk is reached, patients may miss reviews and Northbank’s reputation may be damaged.
items.explanation: This combines a weakness with possible impact — that is risk language.

items.text: The shared training folder allows any Wi-Fi guest to read draft letters.
items.explanation: Over-open permissions are a configuration weakness.

items.text: Ransomware operators targeting health organisations this year.
items.explanation: A threat is a potential source of harm, even before a specific clinic is hit.

items.text: There is a realistic chance that default kiosk logins lead to cancelled appointments and clinical delay.
items.explanation: Likelihood plus impact is risk, not just the weak password itself.

items.text: No check that clinician A is allowed to open patient 1044’s training record.
items.explanation: Missing authorisation is a vulnerability in the application.

items.text: A former contractor still has a live remote-access account they should not have.
items.explanation: An account that was not removed is a control weakness. The person could also be discussed as a threat, but the statement describes leftover access, which is the vulnerability to classify here.

feedback.correct: Those statements match vulnerability, threat or risk.
feedback.incorrect: Ask: is this a weakness, a source of harm, or the chance and impact together?

content.prompt: Write one chain for Northbank: name a vulnerability, a threat that might use it, and the risk (chance and impact) for patients or the organisation. Keep the example fictional.
content.guidance: Use all three terms. Vulnerability = weakness. Threat = who/what might cause harm. Risk = likelihood and impact.

metadata.title: Recognising vulnerability patterns
metadata.summary: Identify common weakness patterns in fictional Northbank examples and explain why they matter.

content.text: Recognising vulnerability patterns

A vulnerability is a weakness in a system, process or configuration that could be used to cause harm. This activity uses simplified, fictional Northbank clinic examples so you can recognise the pattern, explain the possible impact, and name a defensive check. Do not use these ideas against real systems.

Classroom boundary: every snippet is a deliberately weak training example. You are practising identification, detection and secure alternatives — not attacking live services or handling real patient data.

content.prompt: A training booking page still accepts the clinic’s original demo login of admin / admin. What vulnerability pattern is this?

options.label: A legal requirement to keep demo accounts

feedback.correct: Default or shared logins are a vulnerability: they make it too easy for the wrong person to authenticate. A threat is whoever might try; the risk is the chance and impact of that happening at Northbank.
feedback.incorrect: Default or shared logins are a vulnerability: they make it too easy for the wrong person to authenticate. A threat is whoever might try; the risk is the chance and impact of that happening at Northbank.

content.prompt: A fictional records URL is /training/records/patient/1044. The app shows whichever training record matches the number, without checking that the signed-in clinician is allowed to see it. What is the main weakness?

options.label: The clinic uses too many firewalls

feedback.correct: If the app trusts an identifier in the URL and does not also check authorisation, one user may reach another patient’s training record. Detection: review whether every record lookup also checks ownership or role.
feedback.incorrect: If the app trusts an identifier in the URL and does not also check authorisation, one user may reach another patient’s training record. Detection: review whether every record lookup also checks ownership or role.

content.prompt: A Northbank training lookup is built as: query = "SELECT * FROM training_patients WHERE surname = '" + typedSurname + "'". What pattern should you flag?

options.label: Untrusted input concatenated into a query
Asking the learner to type a surname

feedback.correct: Joining untrusted text into a query string can change what the lookup does. Do not try this against real systems. Detection: look for string-built SQL. Remediation: use a parameterised query so the surname is data, not code.
feedback.incorrect: Joining untrusted text into a query string can change what the lookup does. Do not try this against real systems. Detection: look for string-built SQL. Remediation: use a parameterised query so the surname is data, not code.

content.prompt: A fictional training config contains CLINIC_DEMO_TOKEN = "not-a-real-secret" in a file that is copied into the learner hub. Why is this a vulnerability pattern?

options.label: Secrets in source or config can be reused if the file leaks
Tokens should always be printed on posters
Demo tokens cannot be misused even if copied
This is only a threat, not a weakness

feedback.correct: Hard-coded credentials are a weakness in how secrets are stored. If the file is copied, the token travels with it. Detection: search repos for token-like assignments. Fix: store secrets in a secret manager or environment the app reads at run time, and rotate anything that leaked.
feedback.incorrect: Hard-coded credentials are a weakness in how secrets are stored. If the file is copied, the token travels with it. Detection: search repos for token-like assignments. Fix: store secrets in a secret manager or environment the app reads at run time, and rotate anything that leaked.

content.prompt: Northbank’s training kiosk still runs last year’s unpatched booking component after a vendor published a fix. What is the vulnerability?

options.label: Asking reception staff to reboot weekly

feedback.correct: Known, unfixed weaknesses in software are vulnerabilities. A threat is anyone who tries to use that known gap. Impact at a clinic can include disrupted bookings or exposed records. Detection: inventory versions and compare them with vendor advisories.
feedback.incorrect: Known, unfixed weaknesses in software are vulnerabilities. A threat is anyone who tries to use that known gap. Impact at a clinic can include disrupted bookings or exposed records. Detection: inventory versions and compare them with vendor advisories.

content.prompt: A feedback box does comments.innerHTML = visitorMessage in a training page. What is the main client-side risk?

options.label: Untrusted text can be treated as HTML in the page
The page uses too much CSS

feedback.correct: Putting untrusted strings into HTML can change the page for other users. Detection: look for innerHTML, document.write or unsafe templating with user text. Secure alternative: textContent or a library that encodes output.
feedback.incorrect: Putting untrusted strings into HTML can change the page for other users. Detection: look for innerHTML, document.write or unsafe templating with user text. Secure alternative: textContent or a library that encodes output.

content.prompt: A shared training folder is set so that anyone on the clinic Wi-Fi can read every file, including draft letters. What configuration weakness is this?

options.label: Encrypting the letters after they are posted

feedback.correct: Over-permissive shares are a configuration vulnerability: more people can read data than the job requires. Detection: review share permissions and group membership. Control: least privilege and separate staff / visitor networks.
feedback.incorrect: Over-permissive shares are a configuration vulnerability: more people can read data than the job requires. Detection: review share permissions and group membership. Control: least privilege and separate staff / visitor networks.

content.prompt: Which check best detects several of these weaknesses before they reach live clinic systems?

options.label: A code and configuration review against a short secure-coding checklist
Waiting until a patient reports a problem
Deleting logs each night so there is nothing to review
Checking only that the page loads in one browser

feedback.correct: Reviews, dependency/version checks, and secret scanning are detection approaches. They do not replace patching, access control or input validation — they help you find those gaps while the example is still in training data.
feedback.incorrect: Reviews, dependency/version checks, and secret scanning are detection approaches. They do not replace patching, access control or input validation — they help you find those gaps while the example is still in training data.

content.guidance: Name the pattern, the impact, and a detection check. Stay with the fictional clinic examples.

metadata.title: Ethical, Unlawful, Both or Neither
metadata.summary: Classify scenarios as unethical, unlawful, both, or neither.

content.text: Ethical, Unlawful, Both or Neither
Classify each scenario using the four categories. Ethics and law are related but not identical. Some scenarios need more facts before a firm legal conclusion.

content.prompt: Classify each scenario.

items.text: A Northbank receptionist reads a celebrity patient record out of curiosity, with no clinical need and no permission.
items.explanation: Ethically, this breaches trust and confidentiality expectations. Legally, unauthorised access to personal data may engage current United Kingdom data protection legislation and possibly Computer Misuse Act 1990, depending on authorisation and intent. More facts may be needed for a firm legal conclusion.

items.text: An authorised penetration tester runs agreed tests only on systems listed in the signed scope during the agreed window.
items.explanation: With permission, scope and rules of engagement, this is authorised security testing. It is not unethical hacking and is not unlawful in that context.

items.text: A student downloads a password-cracking tool from the internet to try on a friend home router without the friend knowledge.
items.explanation: Ethically, this violates consent and privacy. Unauthorised access attempts may breach the Computer Misuse Act 1990, depending on authorisation and intent. Obtaining a tool intending to use it for misuse may also engage the Computer Misuse Act articles offence inserted by the Police and Justice Act 2006. Possessing legitimate authorised security testing tools is not automatically unlawful.

items.text: Northbank publishes a clear fair-processing notice explaining that access logs may be reviewed after a suspected insider breach.
items.explanation: Transparent, proportionate monitoring communication supports ethical practice and aligns with data protection expectations. This is not inherently unethical or unlawful.

items.text: A manager secretly installs keylogging software on all staff machines indefinitely, including break rooms, with no security incident reason.
items.explanation: Ethically, this is disproportionate and invasive. Legally, covert excessive monitoring may engage data protection and employment law issues. More organisational context may be needed for a precise legal label.

items.text: A researcher publicly releases a Northbank exploit with no prior warning one hour after discovery.
items.explanation: This fails responsible disclosure ethics and may harm patients and staff. Whether it is unlawful depends on what was accessed and how. Do not assume ethics and law always align without facts.

items.text: An employee uses their own credentials to export patient lists they are not permitted to access, then sells the data.
items.explanation: Clearly unethical misuse of trust. Unauthorised access and misuse of personal data likely engages Computer Misuse Act 1990 and current United Kingdom data protection legislation.

items.text: Northbank requires staff to complete annual cyber security awareness training during paid working time.
items.explanation: Training during paid time is a reasonable organisational expectation. It is not unethical and is not unlawful merely because staff must attend.

feedback.correct: Those scenarios match the expected ethical and legal categories.
feedback.incorrect: Check whether each scenario is mainly unethical, unlawful, both, or neither — and whether you have enough facts for a firm legal label.
